title: Joy Comes in the Morning
superscription: A Psalm. A song for the dedication of the temple. Of David.

verses.text: I will exalt You, O LORD, for You have lifted me up and have not allowed my foes to rejoice over me.
O LORD my God, I cried to You for help, and You healed me.
O LORD, You pulled me up from Sheol; You spared me from descending into the Pit.
Sing to the LORD, O you His saints, and praise His holy name.
For His anger is fleeting, but His favor lasts a lifetime. Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning.
In prosperity I said, "I will never be shaken."
O LORD, You favored me; You made my mountain stand strong. When You hid Your face, I was dismayed.
To You, O LORD, I called, and I begged my Lord for mercy:
"What gain is there in my bloodshed, in my descent to the Pit? Will the dust praise You? Will it proclaim Your faithfulness?
Hear me, O LORD, and have mercy; O LORD, be my helper."
You turned my mourning into dancing; You peeled off my sackcloth and clothed me with joy,
that my heart may sing Your praises and not be silent. O LORD my God, I will give thanks forever.

context.author: The title says “of David” (Hebrew le-David), which can mean by David, for David or about David. Seventy-three psalms carry his name; tradition and the New Testament take many of them as his.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.setting: The title calls it “a song for the dedication of the temple” (literally “the house”). “I will exalt You, O LORD, for You have lifted me up” (v.1). David cried for help, and God healed him and pulled him up from Sheol (vv.2-3). He calls others to praise: “For His anger is fleeting, but His favor lasts a lifetime. Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning” (v.5). He confesses his old pride: “In prosperity I said, I will never be shaken” (v.6), until God hid His face (v.7). He pleaded, “Will the dust praise You?” (v.9), and God answered: “You turned my mourning into dancing; You peeled off my sackcloth and clothed me with joy” (v.11).
context.custom: Mourners wore sackcloth, coarse goat-hair cloth, and sat in ashes; taking it off meant grief was over. A new house was dedicated with a ceremony (Deuteronomy 20:5). Which house the title means is debated: David’s palace (2 Samuel 5:11), the site for the Temple he chose (1 Chronicles 22:1), or a later dedication. Jews read this psalm at Hanukkah, the feast of the rededication of the Temple in 164 BC.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 31 includes the words Jesus spoke as He died: “Into Your hands I commit my spirit.”
context.timelineBible: David’s pride in his strength led to the census and plague of 2 Samuel 24, after which he bought the threshing floor where the Temple would be built; some link this psalm to that story. Jesus promised, “your grief will turn to joy” (John 16:20). Hezekiah, healed from sickness, also said that the dead cannot praise God (Isaiah 38:18-19).

translation.meaning: To heal, make whole. God calls Himself “the LORD who heals you” (Exodus 15:26).
Dancing, a round dance of celebration.
Sackcloth, coarse cloth worn in mourning; the source of English “sack.”

gospelParallels.note: Your grief will turn to joy.

otBackground.note: The plague stops at Araunah’s threshing floor.
I will turn their mourning into joy.

overview.summary: Healed and lifted from the edge of death, David confesses his pride, praises God whose anger lasts a night but favor a lifetime, and dances where he once mourned.

history.t: Of a palace, a temple site or the Temple.
Jews read this psalm at the feast.

archaeology.t: Eilat Mazar proposed the Large Stone Structure in the City of David as his palace; others disagree.
Flat rock floors on hilltops, like Araunah’s.

overview.discussion: “In prosperity I said, I will never be shaken” (v.6). When has success made me forget I depend on God?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-60 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David

historicalImage.caption: King David Playing the Harp, by Gerard van Honthorst (1622, Centraal Museum, Utrecht). Seventy-three psalms carry David’s name in their titles, and 1 Samuel 16:23 remembers him as a skilled player of the lyre.

currentImage.caption: The Stepped Stone Structure on the City of David, the hill David captured and made his capital (2 Samuel 5:6-9). Many archaeologists date it to the 10th or 9th century BC; the dating is debated.
